chunks: Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Masrur (may God have mercy on him) narrated to us. He said: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amir narrated to us from his uncle 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir, from Abu Ahmad Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-Azdi, from al-Fadl ibn Yunus. He said:

Ibn Abi al-'Awja' was one of the students of al-Hasan al-Basri, but he deviated from monotheism. It was said to him: You abandoned the school of your companion and entered into that which has no basis and no reality? He said: My companion was confused — he would argue for free will at one time, and for determinism at another. I do not know that he held any school consistently. He said: He came to Mecca out of rebellion and to denounce the pilgrims. The scholars disliked his questioning them and sitting with them due to the filth of his tongue and the corruption of his conscience. So he came to al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) and sat with him among a group of his peers. Then he said to him: O Abu 'Abdillah! Gatherings are trusts, and whoever has a cough must cough. Do you permit me to speak? Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: Say what you wish.

Ibn Abi al-'Awja' said: How long will you continue treading this threshing floor, taking refuge in this stone, worshipping this House built of bricks and clay, and running around it like a startled camel? Whoever thinks or reflects on this would know that this is an act founded by one who is neither wise nor far-sighted. So speak, for you are the head and the hump of this matter, and your father was its foundation and its order.

Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: He whom God leads astray and blinds in heart finds the truth disagreeable and cannot relish it. Satan becomes his guardian and leads him to the watering holes of destruction without return. This House is one by which God has made His creation His servants, to test their obedience in coming to it. He urged them to venerate it and visit it, and He has made it the station of the Prophets and the qibla of those who pray to Him. It is a branch of His good pleasure and a path that leads to His forgiveness, erected upon the uprightness of perfection and the gathering of greatness. God created it two thousand years before He spread out the Earth. God — the Originator of spirits and forms — is most deserving of being obeyed in what He commands and being heeded in what He prohibits and forbids.

Ibn Abi al-'Awja' said: You have spoken, O Abu 'Abdillah, but you referred to the absent. He said: Woe to you! How can He be absent when He is a witness over His creation, and closer to them than the jugular vein? He hears their speech, sees their persons, and knows their secrets. It is only the creature that, when it moves from a place, another place becomes occupied with it and a place becomes empty of it, so it does not know in the place it has moved to what happened in the place it was in. But as for God, the Mighty, the King, the Requiter — no place is devoid of Him and no place is occupied by Him, so no place is closer to Him than another. And by Him who commissioned him with firm signs and clear proofs, aided him with His support, and chose him to convey His messages — we have affirmed his claim that his Lord sent him and spoke to him.

Ibn Abi al-'Awja' then got up from him and said to his companions: Who threw me into this ocean? I asked you to seek a rug for me, but you threw me onto hot coals! They said: You were nothing but humiliated in his gathering. He said: Indeed, he is the son of the one who shaved the heads of those you see.

key_terms.البيدر: Threshing floor (metaphor used derogatorily for the Ka'ba area)
key_terms.الجبر: Determinism/compulsion (theological position that human acts are compelled by God)
key_terms.الديان: The Requiter / Judge (divine name for God who requits all deeds)
key_terms.القدر: Free will / divine decree (theological position on human choice)
key_terms.حبل الوريد: The jugular vein (Quranic phrase, 50:16, for God's extreme nearness)
key_terms.مناهل الهلكة: Watering holes of destruction (metaphor for paths leading to perdition)

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say to Ibn Abi al-Awja' about God's presence and the Ka'ba?
ai.summary: This narrative recounts a famous encounter between the freethinker and atheist Ibn Abi al-Awja' and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) in Mecca during the Hajj season, around the mid-second century AH. Ibn Abi al-Awja', a former student of al-Hasan al-Basri who had abandoned monotheism, mockingly challenged the Imam about the Ka'ba and the rituals of Hajj. The Imam responded with a profound theological defense of the Ka'ba as a divine institution for testing human obedience, followed by a compelling argument for God's omnipresence — that God is not 'absent' but is closer to creation than the jugular vein, perceiving all things simultaneously unlike a created being constrained by space. Ibn Abi al-Awja' withdrew defeated, admitting to his companions that he had been overwhelmed.
